group_iron_colors <- c(
  "CRC-500" = "#d95f02",
  "CRC-50"  = "#66c2a5",
  "HC-500"  = "#fc8d62",
  "HC-50"   = "#1b9e77"
)

color_df <- 
  iNEXT_input_df %>%
  colnames() %>%
  data.frame()

colnames(color_df)[1] <- "names"

iNEXT_color_df <- 
  color_df %>%
  mutate(
    names = gsub("\\.", "-", names),
    names = gsub("^X", "", names)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    metadata_df %>%
      tibble::rownames_to_column("names") %>%
      mutate(
        names = gsub("\\.", "-", names),
        names = gsub("^X", "", names),
        group_iron = paste(Group, Iron.intake, sep = "-")
      ),
    by = "names"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    data.frame(
      group_iron = names(group_iron_colors),
      plot_color = unname(group_iron_colors)
    ),
    by = "group_iron"
  )
ggiNEXT(iNEXT_data, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q") + 
  scale_color_manual(values = iNEXT_color_df$plot_color) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = iNEXT_color_df$plot_color) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  labs(y = "Effective Number of ASVs", x = "Number of Sequences")

iNEXT_manual_df <- 
  iNEXT_data$iNextEst$size_based %>%
  dplyr::rename(names = Assemblage) %>%
  mutate(
    names = gsub("\\.", "-", names),
    names = gsub("^X", "", names)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    metadata_df %>%
      tibble::rownames_to_column("names") %>%
      mutate(
        names = gsub("\\.", "-", names),
        names = gsub("^X", "", names),
        group_iron = paste(Group, Iron.intake, sep = "-")
      ),
    by = "names"
  )

dim(iNEXT_manual_df)
## [1] 12240    14
iNEXT_manual_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Method == "Rarefaction") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = m, y = qD, color = group_iron, group = names)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_grid(Order.q ~ group_iron, scales = "free") + 
  scale_color_manual(values = group_iron_colors) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(y = "Effective Number of ASVs", x = "Number of Sequences") + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

INTERPRETATION 1:

Both the ggiNEXT and manual rarefaction plots indicate that the sequencing depth here was sufficient. As both figures have most curves rise rapidly at low sequencing depth and then level off, suggesting that samples were sequenced deeply enough to characterize the ASVs. In general, I think it’s valid to make conclusions about richness at q=0, q=1, and q=2, although the platueing is more prominant in q=1 and q=2, while in richness along q=0, mild uptrend reamin observed.

Until this point, I processed all the data in this study. However, starting from alpha diversity, i will only focus on the healthy control mice with 2 iron intake groups, just due to the fact I am only interested in the healthy mice, and do not wish to reproduce their data completely.

#create a seperate df for healthy mice only
alpha_df <- 
  iNEXT_data$AsyEst %>%
  dplyr::rename(names = Assemblage) %>%
  mutate(
    names = gsub("\\.", "-", names),
    names = gsub("^X", "", names)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    metadata_df %>%
      tibble::rownames_to_column("names") %>%
      mutate(
        names = gsub("\\.", "-", names),
        names = gsub("^X", "", names)
      ),
    by = "names"
  )

healthy_df <- alpha_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Group == "HC", Diversity == "Species richness")

healthy_shannon_df <- alpha_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Group == "HC", Diversity == "Shannon diversity")

healthy_simpson_df <- alpha_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Group == "HC", Diversity == "Simpson diversity")

# Normality tests
shapiro.test(as.numeric(healthy_df$Observed[healthy_df$Iron.intake == 50]))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  as.numeric(healthy_df$Observed[healthy_df$Iron.intake == 50])
## W = 0.97257, p-value = 0.7305
shapiro.test(as.numeric(healthy_df$Observed[healthy_df$Iron.intake == 500]))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  as.numeric(healthy_df$Observed[healthy_df$Iron.intake == 500])
## W = 0.96662, p-value = 0.538
shapiro.test(as.numeric(healthy_shannon_df$Observed[healthy_shannon_df$Iron.intake == 50]))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  as.numeric(healthy_shannon_df$Observed[healthy_shannon_df$Iron.intake == 50])
## W = 0.90437, p-value = 0.02667
shapiro.test(as.numeric(healthy_shannon_df$Observed[healthy_shannon_df$Iron.intake == 500]))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  as.numeric(healthy_shannon_df$Observed[healthy_shannon_df$Iron.intake == 500])
## W = 0.94364, p-value = 0.164
shapiro.test(as.numeric(healthy_simpson_df$Observed[healthy_simpson_df$Iron.intake == 50]))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  as.numeric(healthy_simpson_df$Observed[healthy_simpson_df$Iron.intake == 50])
## W = 0.87991, p-value = 0.008276
shapiro.test(as.numeric(healthy_simpson_df$Observed[healthy_simpson_df$Iron.intake == 500]))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  as.numeric(healthy_simpson_df$Observed[healthy_simpson_df$Iron.intake == 500])
## W = 0.9058, p-value = 0.02115
# t-tests
ttest_richness <- healthy_df %>%
  t_test(Observed ~ Iron.intake) %>%
  add_y_position(fun = "max")

ttest_shannon <- healthy_shannon_df %>%
  wilcox_test(Observed ~ Iron.intake) %>%
  add_y_position(fun = "max")

ttest_simpson <- healthy_simpson_df %>%
  wilcox_test(Observed ~ Iron.intake) %>%
  add_y_position(fun = "max")

# View results
ttest_richness

The diversity in groups are not all normal, richeness is normal, use t.test. Shannon and simpson are not normal and will use wilcox.test instead of t_test.

### Alpha diversity: Healthy mice only (50 vs 500 iron)

# Species richness only
healthy_df <- alpha_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Group == "HC", Diversity == "Species richness")

# Welch two-sample t-test
ttest_iron <- healthy_df %>%
  t_test(Observed ~ Iron.intake) %>%
  add_y_position(fun = "max")

ttest_iron
## # A tibble: 1 × 10
##   .y.      group1 group2    n1    n2 statistic    df     p y.position groups    
##   <chr>    <chr>  <chr>  <int> <int>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl> <named li>
## 1 Observed 50     500       24    26     -1.41  46.8 0.165       165. <chr [2]>
# Boxplot
iron_ggboxplot <- 
ggboxplot(
  healthy_df,
  x = "Iron.intake",
  y = "Observed",
  color = "Iron.intake",
  fill = "Iron.intake",
  alpha = 0.3,
  outlier.shape = NA
) +
geom_jitter(width = 0.15) +
stat_pvalue_manual(ttest_iron, label = "p") +
scale_color_manual(values = c("50" = "#1b9e77", "500" = "#fc8d62")) +
scale_fill_manual(values = c("50" = "#1b9e77", "500" = "#fc8d62")) +
labs(
  y = "Observed ASV Richness",
  x = "Iron Intake"
) +
theme_bw() +
theme(legend.position = "none")

iron_ggboxplot

alpha_plot_df <- alpha_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Group == "HC") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Order.q = dplyr::case_when(
      Diversity == "Species richness"  ~ "0",
      Diversity == "Shannon diversity" ~ "1",
      Diversity == "Simpson diversity" ~ "2"
    )
  )

alpha_plot_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Iron.intake), y = Observed,
             fill = factor(Iron.intake),
             color = factor(Iron.intake))) + 
  facet_wrap(. ~ Order.q, scales = "free_y") + 
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("50" = "#1b9e77", "500" = "#fc8d62")) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("50" = "#1b9e77", "500" = "#fc8d62")) + 
  labs(y = "Effective Number of ASVs", x = "Iron Intake") + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

###INTERPRETATION 2: If you have categorical data, what can you conclude regarding the role that all ASVs (richess, q = 0) versus common ASVs (Shannon, q = 1) versus dominant ASVs (Simpson, q = 2) have on the biodiversity of your samples as it relates to your variable of interest? For q = 0, the high iron group appeared to have a higher median observed ASV richness than the 50 iron group; however, the difference was not statistically significant, as shown in the previous boxplot (p=0.165). For q = 1 and q = 2, similar visual shifts may suggest changes in common or dominant taxa, but conclusions should depend on their corresponding statistical tests rather than visual inspection alone. Overall, while higher iron intake may show a trend toward increased diversity, none of the alpha diversity test reached statistical significance. Thus, we accept the null hypothesis that the high iron and low iron intake did not alter the gut microbiota in healthy mice.

###INTERPRETATION 3: How did you statistically test your scientific question in Interpretation #2? Why? I used t test for richeness, and then Wilcoxon rank-sum test for simpson and shannon because the diervsity for richeness in groups was normal, but in simpson and shannon indices were not normally distritbuted. Considering i only have 2 test groups to compare for diff, I used parameter and non-parametric t test accrodingly.
